Network Node Analysis
Offline interactive charts

We built a network and then found “communities”

This site turns your diffusion dataset into a network. Each user is a node. A directed edge (u → v) means u spreaded content that originated from v.
We then use community detection to split the network into groups (“communities”). Finally, we answer three questions using plain-English network measures.
What this page answers (Q1–Q3 + Time)
Q1: Key spreaders
Who are the most likely candidate spreaders? (ranking bar + core-vs-bridge scatter + table)
Q2: Community structure
Is the network split into communities, and how concentrated are interactions inside them?
Q3: Inter-community interaction
Which communities exchange the strongest diffusion traffic? (heatmap + top flows)
Time (if available)
When is diffusion most within-community concentrated, and when is activity highest across time bins?

What are nodes, edges, and communities?

Nodes
Each node is a user. We use network structure to identify which users are “candidates” for spreading influence.
Edges
An edge represents diffusion (retweeter → parent). We build a directed network with weights derived from your chosen weight mode.
Communities
Communities are groups of users that connect to each other more than to outsiders. We use community detection to reveal these groups.
Main settings for the site: Weight = count, Filtering = largest connected component (LCC = yes), Community graph = undirected collapsed.
Time bin clarification: We currently have time_elapsed, so time is shown as early→late bins (process stages), not direct clock-hour (0-23).
Key metrics: PageRank indicates “connected influence”; Betweenness identifies nodes that link different parts of the network; Out-degree counts how many diffusion links leave a node.
Important: These are structural indicators (not causal). “Key spreaders” are candidates, not confirmed causes.

Q1 Key Spreaders (candidate)

Question: Which users are the most likely “candidate spreaders” based on network position (not causality)?
Use the algorithm selector to switch results. Hover to see node details. A static PNG fallback is provided below the chart.
Algorithm:
Showing top 50 candidates.
Footer: Bar chart ranks candidates by a composite “structural spreader” score that combines out-degree + PageRank (Brin and Page 1998) + bridge strength to other communities + betweenness (Freeman 1977). The scatter contrasts core influence (x=PageRank) vs cross-community bridging (y=bridge strength). These are structural indicators, not causal proof.

Q2 Community Structure / Polarization

Question: Is the network meaningfully split into communities, and how concentrated is interaction within groups?
Modularity captures how well communities are separated. Within-share measures whether interaction is mostly inside communities.
Modularity (plain English)
Modularity asks: “Are there more edges within the detected communities than we would expect by chance?” Higher modularity usually means communities are more self-contained. (Newman and Girvan 2004)
Footer: Histogram shows the distribution of community sizes; pie shows within-community concentration (within-share) (Newman and Girvan 2004).

Q3 Inter-Community Interaction

Question: Which communities exchange the strongest diffusion traffic (cross-group interaction)?
Heatmap shows aggregated interaction strengths between communities (top by size). Hover to read values.
Footer: Heatmap highlights which communities interact the most; the table lists the strongest community→community flows driving cross-group diffusion.

Time Time Evolution (within-share)

Question: When does diffusion look most “within-community concentrated”, and which time bins are most active?
What does “time bin” mean?
A time bin is a small time bucket. We sort all events from early to late, then split them into 15 buckets with similar numbers of events. So Bin 1 means “earliest period” and Bin 15 means “latest period”.
This is not the same as clock-hour (0-23). It is designed to show process stages. Clock-hour charts are only reliable when raw timestamps and timezone normalization are available.
Activity over time: which processed bins have more events?
Footer: Top plot shows within-community concentration (within-share). Bottom plot shows activity level (events), so you can spot both “most in-group” periods and “most active” periods.

Comparison Algorithms: what changes?

Interpretation checklist: (1) Compare # of communities, then (2) check within-share, and finally (3) look at modularity to judge separation quality.
At a glance: In these runs, INFOMAP detects the most communities, LEIDEN has the highest within-share, and LEIDEN reaches the highest modularity—so algorithm choice mainly affects how finely the network is split (not whether key groups exist).
What this answers: How finely does the algorithm split the network into groups?
How to read: Compare bar heights; higher bar = more communities.
Result: Best (most communities): INFOMAP.
What this answers: Is interaction mostly within groups vs across groups?
How to read: Bigger % = more within-community interaction.
Result: Best (highest within-share): LEIDEN.
What this answers: How clearly separated are the detected communities?
How to read: Higher bar = clearer separation.
Result: Best (highest modularity): LEIDEN.
